newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil cenbank rejects reports about gov't split. [CORRECTED 23:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Brazil cenbank rejects reports about gov't split. [CORRECTED 23:50 GMT]

text.p: Brazil's Central Bank Tuesday dismissed speculation of a split in the government over economic policy and said it had the full backing of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.

"I only know that I am fortunate to live in a country where the president is an ex-finance minister and the finance minister an ex-Central Bank president," the current Central Bank president, Gustavo Loyola, said.

Loyola was responding to questions about caustic comments attributed to Communications Minister Sergio Motta, criticizing Central Bank Director of International Affairs Gustavo Franco and urging more investment in social projects.
Motta denied making the criticism, though several reporters said they had him recorded on tape.
The ebullient minister, a close friend of Cardoso's, reportedly lashed out at Franco as Brazilian stocks tumbled amid ripples from currency woes in some Asian countries.

"There's no point carrying out stabilization of the economy without having an (economic) development plan (corrects from "stabilization plan"). The Asian currency crisis shows us that Gustavo Franco is wrong," Motta said, according to several local wire reports.
Loyola said Motta's comments, if true, were not a criticism but more probably a reflection of an ongoing debate in the government about how to use privatization receipts.
Motta has defended using privatization receipts for social projects while the Central Bank has stuck to its view the money must be used to retire debt.
President Cardoso, speaking through his spokesman, said he fully supported the Central Bank's foreign exchange and monetary policies.
